description:
This article proposes using Geological Thermal Energy Storage (GeoTES) to manage daily and seasonal energy storage.
We develop an energy storage capacity estimation tool for initial reservoir assessment that focuses on reservoir thermal energy storage (RTES)30,31,34,35,36.
The energy storage capacity is estimated for storage volumes within these formations, demonstrating that terawatt-hours of thermal energy (and electrical energy equivalent) can be stored in each formation.
The electrical energy storage capacity \({E}_{e}\) [TWhe] is given by: $${E}_{e}={E}_{t}{\eta }_{e}$$ (2) Equations 1 and 2 represent upper limits to the energy storage capacity, as they imply all of the thermal energy stored in the liquid and rock is extracted, with the exception of energy losses to the surroundings.
These figures show both the lower bound (liquid energy capacity) and upper bound (liquid and solid energy capacity), as discussed in the Estimation Methods section.
text:
The characteristics of energy generation, storage, and consumption are changing rapidly in the United States. Solar and wind contributed the majority of electricity-generating capacity added in 20251, while 16 GW, 50 GWh of utility-scale battery capacity was installed in 2025, representing a 30% increase from 20242,3. Discharge durations of these batteries do not typically exceed 4 h4 due to current capacity market structures, which provide capacity payments up to 4 h5. As the grid evolves there is an increasing need for storage that can manage winter net peaks5 and provide seasonal energy management. A further challenge is the recent increase in electricity demand in key sectors such as domestic manufacturing (semiconductors and critical minerals), and commercial services (notably data centers)6,7. To meet this demand, grid planners are turning to gas turbine generators, but manufacturers are fully booked out to 2030, and 90% of the orders for GE Vernova are backlogged8. Mitsubishi Heavy Industry signaled that they are not adverse to capacity expansion but any increase in turbine manufacturing would be as lean as possible9. This surge in demand is projected to increase turbine costs to 1,800 $/kW and 2,300 $/kW by 2030 for simple cycle and combined cycle gas turbines, respectively10.

In this changing landscape, there is a growing opportunity for long-duration energy storage (LDES) solutions to deliver value by providing resiliency, reliability, security, and cost savings. The LDES National Consortium defines LDES as storage systems capable of delivering electricity for 10 or more hours11. Long discharge durations are important in addressing daily to seasonal imbalances in variable energy supply and demand and providing reliable energy during multi-day extreme events, such as snowstorms or wildfires. Longer discharge durations enhance reliability, reduce curtailment, and limit reliance on low capacity factor peaking plants12. For example, a recent study found that installing LDES could reduce electricity prices during peak demand by 70% in certain scenarios13.

LDES systems require low costs of energy capacity to affordably deliver long discharge durations, and while electro-chemical battery costs are projected to rapidly reduce towards 100 $/kWhe14, such values will be prohibitively expensive for discharge durations over 12 h15. Therefore, a variety of LDES technologies are under development that address discharge durations from multi-day scales (thermal energy storage, flow batteries, Carnot Batteries, etc.), to seasonal scales (pumped hydroelectric storage, compressed air energy storage, hydrogen). This article proposes using Geological Thermal Energy Storage (GeoTES) to manage daily and seasonal energy storage. Several recent studies suggest that GeoTES is an economically feasible, grid-scale, seasonal energy storage technology16,17,18,19,20,21,22,23. These studies explain how GeoTES can store thermal energy in underground reservoirs, which are accessed by wells (existing or drilled for purpose) that produce and inject water to add and remove energy. Previous work explored methods to achieve high thermal recovery efficiency in GeoTES ( >90%) by “pre-charging” an appropriate volume of the reservoir21. Although the wells have a high capital cost, the cost of energy storage capacity is low because the storage material (the reservoir) is free and economically scalable. GeoTES is consequently suitable for LDES applications where the energy storage capacity cost is a driving factor. Moreover, GeoTES uses existing technologies and expertise from the geothermal and oil and gas industries. The thermal energy stored in GeoTES can be converted into electricity or used directly for thermal applications, such as industrial process heating and cooling, potentially reducing exposure to natural gas price fluctuations and minimizing grid impacts in sectors that are being electrified. By taking advantage of the immense subsurface opportunity, GeoTES has transformative potential for the U.S. energy system.

GeoTES is one of several Underground Thermal Energy Storage (UTES) technologies that are under development24,25. Figure 1 depicts GeoTES alongside other UTES systems and illustrates potential energy sources and applications over a range of temperatures. GeoTES has the flexibility to utilize formations like brackish aquifers or depleted oil and gas fields in sedimentary formations, and couple with a wide range of energy sources. Storage temperatures can range from 0 °C to 300 °C or higher (although high temperatures risk triggering geochemical and mechanical changes in the subsurface26,27), and the stored energy can generate electricity or directly provide thermal energy for industrial uses, district heating and cooling projects, or direct use applications like greenhouses. While the storage temperature range of GeoTES may not satisfy some very high-temperature applications, 33% of industrial heating applications in the United States require temperatures below 100 °C, with another 44% requiring temperatures between 100°C and 500 °C28. In addition, binary geothermal power plants have been developed to generate electricity from fluids over 90 °C23.

Previous work has made a case for the cost-effectiveness and technological soundness of GeoTES29, assessed its suitability in several key regions30,31, and summarized lessons learned from operational installations32,33. However, one barrier to development is the uncertainty and variability of subsurface formations, with a perception that there are limited suitable sites for GeoTES deployment. The scale of energy storage capacity made available by this technology has not yet been quantified. Estimating the availability and storage capacity of candidate GeoTES reservoirs is crucial for site selection and technology valuation. Diverse characteristics within target formations and surrounding subsurface create a complex and dynamic environment, necessitating detailed, site-specific characterization for precise modeling and assessment. However, an initial estimation of a reservoir’s storage capacity can provide insights for early reservoir comparison and site selection.

In this article, we present data to illustrate the extensive availability of formations that may be suitable for GeoTES in the United States. We develop an energy storage capacity estimation tool for initial reservoir assessment that focuses on reservoir thermal energy storage (RTES)30,31,34,35,36. Previous efforts have collected and filtered subsurface data in California and Texas to identify promising GeoTES formations17,37. Building upon this work, we down-select to four reservoirs in California and Texas: these sites are the Antelope Hills and Belridge South depleted oil fields in California and the Yegua-Jackson and Carrizo Wilcox aquifers in Texas. The energy storage capacity is estimated for storage volumes within these formations, demonstrating that terawatt-hours of thermal energy (and electrical energy equivalent) can be stored in each formation. Finally, we approximate the number of wells and costs required to develop a representative GeoTES system, lending perspective to the scale of these systems. This effort establishes the foundation for future work in estimating the grid-scale potential of GeoTES.

The lateral extent of saline reservoirs38 and sedimentary basins39 in the contiguous United States is illustrated in Fig. 2. These types of formations may be suitable for GeoTES due to good permeability and proximity to the surface. The vast extent of these formations indicates that GeoTES could be developed in many regions of the United States. Conventional hydrothermal geothermal systems require the intersection of heat, permeability, and fluid in the subsurface, which constrains the regions where they can be deployed compared to GeoTES. Enhanced geothermal systems (EGS) may be developed over larger areas by using hydraulic fracturing and stimulation to create the required permeability for fluid to be pumped through the reservoir. However, drilling to depths that have sufficient heat can be restrictively expensive in some regions. In comparison, potential GeoTES formations can be found all over the country and at relatively shallow depths. Maps of hydrothermal and EGS favorability are included in the Supplementary Information.

Previous work collected California and Texas formation data from a range of federal, state, and local entities and identified candidate GeoTES reservoirs through a preliminary down-selection process17,37. The work defined threshold criteria for key reservoir and fluid parameters (such as temperature greater than 50 °C, average thickness greater than 45 m, and a porosity of at least 10%) and created a shortlist of 59 suitable depleted oil fields in California and 15 brackish aquifers in Texas. Using the data collected, these sites were further evaluated by estimating their capital costs ($/GJ/m2 of subsurface lateral extent) and self-discharge rate (% annual heat loss in year 10). Figures 3, 4 depict the lateral extent of the most suitable nine and ten sites in California and Texas, respectively, out of those evaluated. Note that the California sites (oil fields) and the Texas sites (brackish aquifers) represent distinct geologic regions. Oil fields can have multiple reservoir units, and aquifers can overlap with multiple formations.

We make a further down-selection in this work to choose two sites in California and two sites in Texas: Belridge South had the lowest self-discharge rate and capital costs of all California sites, and the company Premier Resource Management is developing a demonstration GeoTES project at Antelope Hills. Carrizo-Wilcox and Yegua-Jackson were two of the top three brackish aquifers evaluated in Texas (joined by Dockum), and the Yegua-Jackson formation has been targeted by the company EarthBridge Energy to develop their GeoBattery concept40.

To estimate the energy storage capacity of volumes within these selected formations, subsurface data were collected from several sources, ranging from public databases from the USGS and BRACS to private databases and industry partners. The data are used to evaluate the energy storage capacity of reservoirs with each field and therefore assess their suitability for GeoTES. The GeoTES model uses the structure of the pre-existing geothermal Resource Size Assessment Tool (RSAT)41, which was altered to apply to GeoTES formations, mirroring established methods used for RTES capacity estimation30,34. The GeoTES model estimates the maximum thermal energy capacity \({E}_{t}\) [TWht] of a reservoir using the following equation

$${E}_{t}={hA}\left[\left(1-\varepsilon \right){\rho }_{s}{c}_{s}+\varepsilon {\rho }_{w}{c}_{w}\right]\Delta T{\eta }_{t}$$

(1)

in which h [m] is the formation thickness, ε [−] is the porosity, ρ [kg/m3] is the density, c [J/kg·K] is the specific heat capacity, and subscripts s and w refer to solid and water, respectively. Here, ΔT [°C] is the difference between the reservoir outlet and return temperatures. Storage capacity scales linearly with ΔT, which is dependent on the chosen storage temperature and end-use application. The subsurface area, A, represents the area of the field, reservoir, or fluid accumulation surrounding the sample well within the reservoir. These samples do not represent the entire area of the target storage reservoir. The geothermal recovery factor, \({\eta }_{t}\) [%], represents the fraction of thermal energy that can be recovered from the reservoir after re-injection.

As GeoTES systems can supply thermal energy or electricity to customers, the recoverable electrical storage capacity of the reservoir is also calculated using a thermal-to-electric conversion efficiency, ηe [%], which depends on storage temperature, but is generally <20%. The electrical energy storage capacity \({E}_{e}\) [TWhe] is given by:

$${E}_{e}={E}_{t}{\eta }_{e}$$

(2)

Equations 1 and 2 represent upper limits to the energy storage capacity, as they imply all of the thermal energy stored in the liquid and rock is extracted, with the exception of energy losses to the surroundings. A lower limit is estimated by assuming that the well-field is operated to avoid thermal breakthrough – that is, the fluid temperature at the production well does not vary. For a doublet comprising a production well and an injection well, a thermal gradient (or thermocline) will exist between the wells and will gradually move from the injector to the producer. This thermal gradient moves relatively slowly compared to the fluid velocity, and the ratio of distance covered by the thermal gradient \({d}_{{thermal}}\) [m] compared to the water flow \({d}_{{piston}}\) [m] is given by:

$$\frac{{d}_{{thermal}}}{{d}_{{piston}}}=\sqrt{\frac{\varepsilon {\rho }_{w}{c}_{w}}{\varepsilon {\rho }_{w}{c}_{w}+\left(1-\varepsilon \right){\rho }_{s}{c}_{s}}}$$

(3)

This equation is derived assuming there is no ground-water flow, that the solid and liquid are in thermal equilibrium (a good assumption given the low Biot numbers involved), and that the thermal gradient is a sharp step-function34,42. Derivation of Eq. 3 can be found in the Supplementary Information. In reality, the thermal gradient is not a step function and instead spreads out and steepens up depending on rock properties, temperatures43, and operation44. Nominal reservoir characteristics of ε = 0.3, ρw = 1000 kg/m3, cw = 4200 J/kg·K, ρs = 2350 kg/m3, and cs = 930 J/kg·K leads to a value of \({d}_{{\rm{thermal}}}/{d}_{{\rm{piston}}}=0.67\) meaning that fluid injected at the injector will reach the producer while the thermal front will have progressed 67% of the distance, thereby avoiding thermal breakthrough. Therefore, it is conventional to use the energy stored in the liquid component of the reservoir as a lower bound of the energy capacity31 – i.e.,

$${E}_{t,{\rm{liquid}}}={hA}\varepsilon {\rho }_{w}{c}_{w}\Delta T{\eta }_{t}$$

(4)

Similarly, the lower bound of electrical energy capacity is given by

$${E}_{e,{\rm{liquid}}}={\eta }_{e}{E}_{t,{\rm{liquid}}}$$

(5)

The number of wells \({N}_{{well}}\) and their cost can be estimated with a simple model that compares the energy delivered per well \({E}_{{well}}\,[{{\rm{TWh}}}_{{\rm{t}}}]={\dot{m}}_{{well}}{c}_{w}\Delta T{\tau }_{{dis}}\) to the total energy extracted from the GeoTES (Eqs. 1 and 4), where \({\dot{m}}_{{well}}\) [kg/s] is the mass flow rate of each well and \({\tau }_{{dis}}\) [s] is the discharge duration. The number of wells per unit energy stored is given by

$$\frac{{N}_{{well}}}{{E}_{t}}=\frac{2}{{\dot{m}}_{{well}}{\tau }_{{dis}}{c}_{w}\Delta T}$$

(6)

The 2 in the numerator reflects that both production and injection wells are required. The total cost of wells per unit energy \({C}_{{\rm{total}}}/{E}_{t}\) is estimated using an assumed capital cost to drill and install pumps at each well, \(\bar{C}\) [USD]

$$\frac{{C}_{\mathrm{total}}}{{E}_{t}}=\frac{2\bar{C}}{{\dot{m}}_{{well}}{\tau }_{{dis}}{c}_{w}\Delta T}$$

(7)

in which \(\bar{C}\) is the estimated cost to drill and install pumps at each well and is assumed to range from $750,000–$1,250,000 (note, these wells are likely to be less deep than conventional geothermal wells).

It should be noted that Eqs. 6 and 7 are valid for both upper and lower bound estimates of GeoTES energy storage capacity. Derivation of Eqs. 6 and 7 can be found in the Supplementary Information, along with further information on data sources and assumed values for each parameter (including conversion efficiency).

There is considerable uncertainty and variability for each parameter, which can significantly affect estimates of storage capacity and cost. For example, only three data points were available to inform the inputs for the Belridge South site, while over 500 data points were available for both Carrizo-Wilcox and Yegua-Jackson reservoirs. Furthermore, while the subsurface area of a reservoir, such as those selected aquifers in Texas, may be vast, only a fraction of this area may possess all the favorable characteristics required for GeoTES. The area data used in this analysis are from wells drilled in a selection of fields that are part of larger plays, aquifers, or reservoirs. These plays and aquifers may span different formations and contain many different fields that may or may not overlap in some capacity. These areas do not represent the entire case study oil fields or aquifers in their sum. Nevertheless, the vast available area supports potential project expansion and grid-scale systems.

As a result of this uncertainty, a Monte Carlo approach is taken. Each parameter is assumed to vary with an appropriate probability distribution (such as triangular, normal, lognormal, uniform, and constant). The Monte-Carlo simulation evaluates the model 10,000 times, each time randomly sampling each probability distribution to build a distribution of expected energy capacity and cost. This method provides a range of estimated capacity values in which statistical probability can be assessed, rather than just a single value.

The thermal and electricity energy storage capacities of the storage volumes within the four selected reservoirs are shown in Figs. 5, 6, respectively. These figures show both the lower bound (liquid energy capacity) and upper bound (liquid and solid energy capacity), as discussed in the Estimation Methods section. The thermal storage capacities are consistently larger by about one order of magnitude than electrical capacities, reflecting the application of the thermal-to-electric conversion efficiency factor. Results show considerable variation in the energy storage capacity within and between each formation. This spread is due primarily to the uncertainty in the reservoir area, which varies significantly across and within sites. Each reservoir characteristic has a linear impact on capacity (see Eq. 1), and because the area has the largest magnitude and variation, it has the greatest impact on the range of estimates. Another important reservoir property is the heat capacity of the rock. One study of UTES systems found that when the heat capacity of a saturated formation is normalized for porosity, the rock, not the fluid, stores most of the energy. The fluid primarily serves as a heat-transfer medium, conveying heat between the subsurface and surface components45. Despite this, mean values are consistently on the order of several terawatt-hours indicating the vast storage potential and impact that GeoTES in individual formations could have.

The shaded regions in Figs. 5, 6 indicate the distribution of the Monte Carlo results. The results of Belridge South show a symmetrical, almost normal distribution, reflecting the balanced triangular distribution of its inputs. In contrast, Antelope Hills, Yegua-Jackson, and Carrizo-Wilcox have asymmetrical, nearly lognormal distributions, reflecting their bottom-heavy triangular distributions for area and thickness inputs. This suggests most target storage volumes in these formations have capacities below the mean. On the other hand, however, when reservoir and fluid properties align to create ideal storage conditions, capacities can exceed 3000 TWhth.

Table 1 shows the average storage capacity estimates for each site. It should be noted that the results reflect the storage capacity of discrete volumes within each reservoir. The area and thickness data available do not describe the entire reservoir, but rather the volumes of selected pools and fields within the target formations. The effect of this is seen in the fact that the fields in Yegua-Jackson, a massive aquifer spanning Texas, had a smaller estimated capacity than those in Belridge South, a relatively small oil field. The average area and thickness of the selected sites in Yegua-Jackson are smaller than those of Belridge South. In reality, the entirety of Yegua-Jackson has a storage capacity far above Belridge South. Nonetheless, the results suggest massive storage capacities available at each site.

Developing a large-scale GeoTES system requires numerous wells to be drilled, and the number of wells and their cost can be estimated using Eqs. 6 and 7. A 1 TWhth GeoTES system with a 1000 h discharge duration requires between 24 and 190 wells, depending on the assumed value of permeability, well flow rate, and formation thickness (input assumptions are given in the Supplementary Information). Drilling this many wells is achievable given current industry drilling rates: between September 2024 and September 2025, nearly 12,000 new wells were drilled in the contiguous United States, with 424 drilled in August 2025 in the Permian Basin46. Therefore, the knowledge and workforce currently exist to drill hundreds of wells in a single region in a short time. Assuming a cost per well in the range of $750,000 to $1,250,000 leads to a GeoTES capital cost between 0.018 and 0.239 $/kWhth. Converting thermal energy to electricity would increase the cost by an order of magnitude, reflecting the thermal-to-electric conversion efficiency. GeoTES costs in this range – approximately 0.2–2.5 $/kWhe – are competitive compared to other electricity storage technologies such as utility-scale battery storage (ranging from about 66 to 477 $/kWhe47,48). While this is a capital cost, not a levelized cost, the cost of drilling is a driving cost component in GeoTES systems and thus gives an initial insight into their magnitude. Similarly, delivering 1 TWhe of electrical capacity with GeoTES would require 240–1,900 wells which is also feasible given the drilling rates above.

text:
Data centers are coming to Michigan — construction has started on major projects and the state is being eyed for further development as demand for artificial intelligence processing grows.

But not everyone is happy about it. Although some in state government have pointed to hyperscale data centers as an economic driver for Michigan's future, others are concerned about how they'll affect water, energy and other parts of the communities they're being placed in.

Awareness of data centers is becoming commonplace — a survey conducted by Pew Research Center found 75% of Americans have either heard a little or a lot about data centers. And with voters in Michigan picking a new governor this fall, it's an issue likely to come up on the election trail.

Among major gubernatorial candidates, a theme has emerged when it comes to data centers: the facilities have the potential to bring jobs to Michigan, particularly in the construction phase, but those campaigning for the state's top office say the companies operating data centers must ensure they pay for the energy they consume and not threaten natural resources, namely water.

Jocelyn Benson, Democrat

Benson, currently secretary of state, said data center projects coming to Michigan have the potential for "creating good-paying union jobs" but contends that developers must operate responsibly. Her campaign said data centers must pay for the energy they use. Before they can be built, developers have to show their projected water and land usage to prevent overburdening the state's natural resources.

"As governor, I’ll implement standards and guardrails to shape projects, and ensure a transparent process that involves impacted communities, so we can drive economic development while also embracing opportunities to support our clean-energy and power grid buildout," Benson said in a statement provided by her campaign.

She also called for public hearings for residents to provide input on projects, as well as public disclosures from developers operating data centers.

Benson’s husband, Ryan Friedrichs, is a vice president at Related Companies, parent company of a developer behind a hyperscale data center campus slated for Saline Township. Friedrichs said in a March LinkedIn post he is no longer working on any Michigan-based projects, having stepped into a national stakeholder advocacy position at Related Companies.

Mike Cox, Republican

Cox, a former Michigan Attorney General, also believes data center developers must pay for the energy they use. He also said at an April 24 forum hosted by the Michigan Press Association that the state should continue to allow for local decision-making when it comes to data centers, and communities that would like to host should be allowed to.

"Local control has not been taken away in regards to data centers," Cox said. "Every single community has the ability to put a moratorium on them. I'd encourage every single community to exercise local control."

Mike Duggan, independent

A spokesperson for Duggan's campaign said the former Detroit mayor would create rules for data centers looking to operate in Michigan: mandated public transparency agreements for developers; operators having to pay the complete cost of energy needed for the facilities; and using less water-intensive closed-loop cooling systems.

"As governor, Mike Duggan will establish a single standard for data center siting in Michigan and will provide legal assistance to local communities to support each community's local decision," Duggan spokesperson Andrea Bitely said. "No community will be bullied into a data center."

John James, Republican

James, currently a member of Congress, said data centers coming to Michigan should be mindful of concerns about water usage, and also said that the facilities should not lead to a wide reduction in available farmland in Michigan. Following the State of the State event in Lansing on Feb. 25, James told reporters that existing brownfield sites could offer alternative sites for data centers.

"We have to take care of our water," James said. "I say all the time Michigan is open for business, but we are not for sale. If a company comes and they need power, we'll sell it to them. But if you go over and it increases rates, you're going to pay for it."

Perry Johnson, Republican

Johnson, a businessman, noted at the MPA forum that energy costs have been steadily increasing in Michigan. He said data center developers should invest in Michigan's energy infrastructure to avoid passing on costs to ratepayers.

"Let's be realistic, this is unbearable," Johnson said, of energy costs. "If they are going to make all that money, they should at least have to make an investment."

Aric Nesbitt, Republican

Nesbitt, who is the Republican leader in the Michigan Senate, said March 9 there should be no state incentives given to tech companies looking to bring data centers to Michigan.

"Big tech has enough money to build it themselves, they don't need subsidies from Lansing or hard-working taxpayers," Nesbitt told reporters following an event in Grand Rapids.

He also said there must be "ironclad agreements" between developers and energy providers that data center developers pay the full cost for energy and that energy rates do not increase as a result of data centers being brought online. He also called for closed-loop water systems. Finally, Nesbitt said the state should not intervene in local decision-making about data centers.

Chris Swanson, Democrat

Swanson, who is sheriff in Genesee County, said at the MPA forum that local residents must have a say when developers want to open data centers in their communities.

"You and I have a place that we live, and we're proud of it. We want our communities to be protected," he said.

He also said Michigan should not offer tax credits and incentives to developers, but communities that want to have manufacturing sectors and can provide infrastructure needed for data centers should be allowed to host them.

text:
A recent report by the Pelican Institute for Public Policy provides a case study on the influence of nonprofit-networks, funded by a small set of powerful foundations, on public policy in Louisiana.

Barriers to Louisiana Energy Dominance outlines, beyond legal and regulatory factors, a “sophisticated network of advocacy organizations” and the methods by which it influences the public, policymakers, and energy production. Some of the more striking takeaways from the report includes a claim of Chinese communist influence, one rather Machiavellian public influence campaign, and Michael Bloomberg’s role in Louisiana state and local policy.

The network

The report centers its analysis on a coalition known as Louisianans Against False Solutions (LAFS), a group of nonprofits advocating for a transition away from fossil fuels. According to the study, twelve Louisiana-based members of this coalition collectively received at least $115.5 million in funding since 2020, 98.4 percent of which originated outside of the state. Members of LAFS include Deep South Center for Environmental Justice, Taproot Earth, and Alliance for Affordable Energy.

These networks are intricate. Multiple LAFS members are fiscally sponsored projects of other organizations; others are networks themselves of nonprofits. LAFS itself is a fiscally sponsored project of the Foundation for Louisiana.

The funders

The study identifies the top 30 donors to Louisiana-based LAFS members. The five with the largest contributions are:

Waverley Street Foundation:- $15.3 million

Windward Fund (part of the Arabella Network, now Sunflower Services) – $9.8 million

Robert Wood Johnson Foundation – $8 million

Freedom Together Foundation – $6.5 million

Amalgamated Charitable Foundation Inc. – $6.5 million

They are familiar names, frequently identified in CRC and InfluenceWatch research for their role in funding left-of-center policy advocacy. The list continues among the likes of the Ford Foundation, W.K. Kellogg Foundation, Silicon Valley Community Foundation, and Tides Foundation.

The methods

This network influences Louisiana energy policy through shaping public opinion, lobbying policymakers, and litigation.

The report places particular emphasis on a subset of local organizations that present themselves as conservative while opposing energy development broadly. It points to the Louisiana CO2 Alliance and its affiliated coalition, Save My Louisiana, as examples. These groups present themselves as conservative, while reportedly coordinating with left-of-center and national anti–fossil fuel organizations such as the Sierra Club and the Bold Alliance. In one instance, a board member of Save My Louisiana was identified participating in a strategy call with activists discussing how to jointly oppose energy infrastructure projects. To appeal to conservative audiences, advocacy groups such as Louisiana CO2 Alliance frame messaging around property rights, local control, and opposition to corporate welfare.

Groups within the network “maintain sophisticated media operations” that provide local journalists ready-made materials that make it easier to frame Louisiana energy issues in terms of environmental injustice, climate harm, or corporate malfeasance. Some groups fund journalism projects on these issues directly.

Alliance for Affordable Energy and others lobby the Louisiana Public Service Commission and in legislative debates, advocating renewable energy mandates, efficiency programs, and tighter limits on traditional energy development.

A further, rather prominent method is litigation and legal pressure. The report highlights organizations such as the Deep South Center for Environmental Justice, Healthy Gulf, Louisiana Environmental Action Network, and Rise St. James for creating and supporting legal challenges that slow, raise the cost of, or block energy development altogether.

Bloomberg

According to the report, Michael Bloomberg has spent more than building a national network that operates directly in state and local policy. In Louisiana, Bloomberg-backed funding supports similar initiatives.

“Direct government integration,” as the report describes it, is one facet of the strategy. Bloomberg-funded programs place fellows inside state and local agencies, embedding externally funded staff within public institutions to advance Bloomberg policy priorities. These programs also provide “free” technical assistance, data analysis, and policy development support. In New Orleans, the city engaged extensively with Bloomberg climate initiatives through its Office of Resilience and Sustainability, receiving technical support from the National Renewable Energy Laboratory and participating in Bloomberg’s broader city network initiatives including C40 Cities and the Global Covenant of Mayors. Through this support, the city adopted a Climate Action Plan with targets including net zero emissions by 2050 and 100 percent clean electricity by 2035.

Energy Foundation China, Earthjustice and foreign influence

The report outlines the network’s connection to Energy Foundation China (EFC) and U.S. Energy Foundation (EF), which are facing—according to the report—“intense scrutiny” over alleged ties to the Chinese Communist Party.

EFC and EF are nominally distinct organizations. However, they were previously the same legal entity before splitting in 2019. The report notes shared office space into 2022 and shared personnel through at least 2024. The foundations have been accused of moving millions to US-based organizations to advance Chinese energy policies and “climate lawfare aimed at weakening the United States.” Six of the twelve Louisiana-based LAFS groups have received a total of $6.4 million from EFC and EF.

The climate litigation group Earthjustice sits at the center of this network, with ties to EFC and EF, Michael Bloomberg, and the Louisiana advocacy networks such as LAFS. Employing 220 lawyers and engaged in 680 active legal cases, it maintains an active role in Louisiana, representing local activist groups in lawsuits, permit challenges, and civil rights complaints. It has received $8.5 million from EFC and EF since 2006, and its leadership overlaps with the network; according to its 2025 Annual Report, Earthjustice’s chair of the board of trustees, Stuart Clarke, also serves as board chair for EF.

text:
Bryan County, Georgia, is emerging as a critical hub for the future of U.S. auto manufacturing. Hyundai Motor Group has invested $7.6 billion into its Hyundai Motor Group Metaplant America, a nearly 3,000-acre facility outside Savannah that signals a major shift in how vehicles are built, powered, and delivered.

This is Hyundai’s first dedicated EV and battery plant in the U.S., with initial capacity of 300,000 vehicles annually and the ability to scale to 500,000. It’s designed for efficiency and resilience, using advanced robotics and real-time production systems to improve quality and flexibility. A key advantage is on-site battery production through a joint venture with LG Energy Solution, reducing supply chain risk and tightening control over one of the most critical EV components.

Sign up for CBT News’ daily newsletter and get the latest industry stories delivered straight to your inbox.

The economic impact is significant. Hyundai expects to create more than 8,500 direct jobs and nearly 7,000 additional roles tied to suppliers and logistics, further strengthening its U.S. footprint. Since entering the market in 1986, Hyundai has steadily expanded domestic production, with about 80 percent of its U.S. lineup now built in America.

The MetaPlant will eventually support multiple brands, including Kia and Genesis, creating a flexible, multi-brand production hub. Supporting this is the Hyundai Mobility Training Center, where technicians and engineers receive hands-on training in EV systems, diagnostics, and advanced vehicle technologies to meet growing service demands.

The plant is already producing key models like the 2026 Hyundai IONIQ 5, offering up to 318 miles of range and access to the Tesla Supercharger network through its NACS port. Joining it is the 2026 Hyundai IONIQ 9, a three-row electric SUV with up to 335 miles of range and ultra-fast charging capability from 10 to 80 percent in about 24 minutes.

Looking ahead, Hyundai plans to expand production to include hybrid models and hydrogen fuel cell trucks, reflecting a diversified powertrain strategy. At the same time, the company is investing in autonomy through partnerships with Waymo and Motional, with additional support from Magna International and deployment through Uber.

For dealers, this investment means more stable inventory, faster delivery, and a clearer signal that Hyundai is committed to long-term growth in the U.S. The MetaPlant isn’t just about building EVs, it’s about building a scalable, future-ready manufacturing strategy that aligns with where the industry is heading.

text:
Greetings Agents of Impact!

In today’s Brief:

The data center power equation

All Aboard Coalition’s latest deal

Local, sustainable rare earth refining

How faith-based investors can step up

Featured: Deploy!

Renewable energy gains steam despite headwinds, as energy demand surges. Renewable energy sources are supplying about half of the electricity needed for the new data centers powering the AI revolution. Why not 100%? Power supply is the main constraint. Big tech and data center developers are scrambling to get electricity online as quickly as possible. Increasingly, that energy is generated by solar and wind power, with battery storage to smooth out the variability. Such systems often take the form of “behind-the-meter” energy production, co-located with the data center to avoid permitting and long wait times for grid connections. Renewables are now competitive with new gas on a levelized cost basis, even without subsidies, especially as the costs and wait for gas turbines have ballooned due to supply chain constraints, according to BloombergNEF. “The fastest and cheapest way to deploy energy today is through clean energy,” Majid Al Suwaidi of Alterra, the UAE’s $30 billion climate fund, said at the recent BNEF conference in New York, where AI-driven energy demand dominated the discussions.

Firm power. The massive renewables buildout represents an inflection point in the deployment of clean energy generation, which has been growing rapidly despite political headwinds. Yet even with the cost advantage of solar and wind, natural gas still captures half of data center demand. Eleven gas-fired data centers being built by companies including xAI, Meta, Microsoft and OpenAI will generate as much greenhouse gas emissions as some countries, a Wired analysis found. One reason behind gas’s appeal: the need for so-called firm power that can run reliably 24/7 and ramp up or down as needed. The default for such “baseload” energy is natural gas; hyperscalers are also lining up hydropower, nuclear energy and even fusion energy. The emergence of long-duration batteries that can store power generated from wind and solar for hours and even weeks is making renewable energy an increasingly viable firm power option, at least with grid or natural gas backup. “If you look at just our financing pipeline, renewable energy and storage – being that it’s still much faster and cleaner and cheaper – represents a lot of the new generation pipeline,” said Karen Fang of Bank of America.

Ready-to-scale. Climate investment trends reflect the shift from early stage innovation to ready-to-scale deployments. Clean energy, energy efficiency and industrial electrification drove global energy transition investment to a record $2.3 trillion in 2025, up 8% from the prior year, according to BNEF. Early-stage climate tech deals, on the other hand, fell to their lowest level since 2020 according to a separate tally from Sightline Climate. Before they can be widely deployed, climate tech startups have to make the jump from promising technology to revenue-generating commercial production. That involves building their first plants, which are typically as novel as the technology they aim to produce. With the retreat of Breakthrough Energy Catalyst, a key first-of-a-kind, or FOAK, funder, the gap has become more acute. “Without that bridge to bankability for those FOAK projects, we delay resilient energy systems, domestic manufacturing, and local job creation,” Elemental Impact’s Dawn Lippert told ImpactAlpha.

Keep reading, “Renewable energy gains steam despite headwinds, as energy demand surges,” by Amy Cortese and Erik Stein.

Dealflow: Low-Carbon Transition

All Aboard Fund backs ready-to-scale green cement maker Terra. An investment collaborative created to mobilize capital for ready-to-scale climate tech startups has made a $22 million investment in Terra, a green cement maker building its first commercial-scale production plant. It’s the second investment by the All Aboard Coalition, which was launched last year by investor and former TED curator Chris Anderson and more than two dozen climate tech investment firms to fill a funding gap for startups ready to commercialize (see, “All Aboard Coalition mobilizes co-investments in climate tech as federal funding falls”). The investment comes after coalition members Breakthrough Energy, Just Climate and GenZero backed the Golden, Colo.-based Terra’s $124.5 million Series B round in July (All Aboard co-invests when three or more of its member firms back a company). The additional funding brings Terra’s B round to $147 million, and will help it construct its plant for low-carbon cement in Celburne, Texas. “Terra is one of the only companies that has moved beyond the lab and built a commercially serious solution at a moment when the industry urgently needs one,” said All Aboard’s Jay Dessy. “Cleburne is the proof point this market has been waiting for.”

Virtuous cycle. The investment by All Aboard is intended to send a signal to other investors that Terra is poised for breakthrough success. In January, the coalition invested in Salt Lake City-based Zanskar, which uses AI to supercharge geothermal exploration and development. The investment was part of Zanskar’s $115 million Series C round to support the development of a multi-gigawatt pipeline of geothermal power plants in the western US. Zanskar last month went on to secure up to $100 million in project financing in a deal led by Just Climate and Spring Lane Capital.

More.

Argentina-based Alkemio closes pre-seed round to localize rare earth mineral refining. Rare earth elements are critical inputs for electric vehicles, wind turbines and smartphones, as well as defense. Yet most global refining happens in China. Alkemio, a Buenos Aires-based startup, has closed a $2 million pre-seed round to advance an organic, modular refining process designed to be used directly at mine sites, cutting the need to ship raw material overseas. The three-year old company says the approach cuts emissions by more than 70% and eliminates toxic solvents. Investors in the round include Mexico City-based Dalus Capital, San Francisco-based VU Venture Partners, Amplifica Capital, Argentinian oil-and-gas corporate venture fund VX Ventures, and Epic Angels. “The world urgently needs the ability to refine rare earths sustainably and reliably, wherever the deposits are,” said Maaike Doyer of Epic Angels. The funding will help Alkemio scale from a lab prototype to pilot project in the US.

Stranded deposits. Conventional rare earth refining generally requires facilities so large they are only economically viable at massive centralized scale. Almost no country outside China has built one. Mining companies across Latin America have begun stockpiling material as trade tensions rise. “Rare earths are called rare, but they are present in almost the entire world, just in low concentrations. Every country is a potential place for a rare earth mine,” Alkemio’s Ailín Svagzdys told ImpactAlpha. With on-site processing, he envisions mining projects across a much broader geography. Given the scramble for such minerals, he added, “it will probably not take as long as people think.” Alkemio has signed letters of intent with mining companies in Latin America, the US and Canada.

More.

Dealflow overflow. Investment news crossing our desks:

Spain’s Solaria raised €300 million ($325 million) to expand its data center and battery storage operations, repositioning itself from a clean energy producer to a critical infrastructure operator in Europe. (Bloomberg)

Octopus Energy Generation committed $500 million to reforestation projects developed by California-based Living Carbon and invested $13 million in the company’s carbon removal business. (Living Carbon)

Copenhagen Infrastructure Partners acquired Ørsted’s European onshore renewable energy business and relaunched it as Perigus Energy. (Copenhagen Infrastructure Partners)

Impact Voices: Faith-Based Investing

How faith-based investors can do more to promote human flourishing. Can faith-aligned investors become known for what they are for, in addition to what they are against? That was the question posed by Martin Palmer, the founding president of FaithInvest and one of the primary conveners of last month’s Faith in the Common Good conference in Paris. For faith-inspired investors, few questions are more important, write Sorenson Impact Group’s Jim Sorenson and Impact Evaluation Lab’s Terrence Keeley in a guest post (disclosure: Sorenson Impact Foundation is an investor in ImpactAlpha). Faith institutions oversee at least $12 trillion in assets. The vast majority of that capital’s values-alignment comes in the form of negative screens for alcohol, tobacco, gambling and other “vice” industries. Sorenson and Keeley came to the conference with a white paper exploring investment strategies that “may promote more heavenly outcomes right here on Earth.” According to a survey of attendees, 90% believe that faith-based investors have unique value to contribute to global capital markets.

World made new. “Our separate faith traditions – the Church of Jesus Christ of Latter Day Saints and Roman Catholicism – have always guided our personal and professional lives,” Sorenson and Keeley write. That belief helped lead Sorenson to align 100% of his foundation’s assets with positive impact beginning in 2017, and to collaborate with Keeley on the launch of Impact Evaluation Lab to measure the authenticity, impact and likely financial returns of such strategies. The Lab has also partnered with Sovereign Capital on a new faith-based impact measurement and management framework. At the conference, Sorenson and Keeley “volunteered to work with other attendees to help promote practical ideas – including better analytics and transactional opportunities,” to align investment capital and religious convictions. The pair say they can “imagine a day not far from now when all investors, perhaps led by the faith-based community, say not only how much their investments have made, but also how much good they have done.”

Keep reading, “How faith-based investors can do more to promote human flourishing,” by Jim Sorenson and Terrence Keeley.
